body: 1992 letter: the two approaches 'are joined at the hip: Growth is always a component in the calculation of value, constituting a variable whose importance can range from negligible to enormous and whose impact can be negative as well as positive'; 'the very term "value investing" is redundant.' Key rule: 'Growth benefits investors only when the business in point can invest at incremental returns that are enticing - in other words, only when each dollar used to finance the growth creates over a dollar of long-term market value. In the case of a low-return business requiring incremental funds, growth hurts the investor.' Example given: airlines - 'The more the industry has grown, the worse the disaster for owners.' He condenses John Burr Williams: value 'is determined by the cash inflows and outflows - discounted at an appropriate interest rate - that can be expected to occur during the remaining life of the asset.' 2000 letter restates via Aesop: 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' - ask how certain the birds are, when and how many, and the risk-free rate. 'Common yardsticks such as dividend yield, the ratio of price to earnings or to book value, and even growth rates have nothing to do with valuation except to the extent they provide clues to the amount and timing of cash flows'; 'growth can destroy value if it requires cash inputs in the early years' that exceed later discounted value; 'Using precise numbers is, in fact, foolish; working with a range of possibilities is the better approach.' Actionable: always pair revenue growth with incremental ROCE; low-P/E/low-P/B is not value by itself.

data.rule: growth adds value only if incremental ROIC > cost of capital

title: Buffett 1992/2000: growth and value are 'joined at the hip'; growth only helps above the cost of capital
